keyVerseText: And her husband went with her along weeping behind her to Bahurim. Then said Abner unto him, Go, return. And he returned. along: Heb. going and weeping
rootMeaning: The root word בָּחוּר (bâchûwr) means 'young man' or 'chosen youth,' emphasizing selection or choice. The plural form בַּחֻרִים (Bachurîym) literally means 'young men' but is used as a proper name for a location. This suggests the place was likely associated with or named after a group characterized by vigor, youthfulness, or being specially chosen. The root's nuance of selection enriches the understanding beyond a simple geographical label, implying a place of significance related to vitality or chosen individuals.
usageInScripture: The term בַּחֻרִים appears five times in Scripture, consistently referring to a town in the territory of Benjamin situated beyond the Mount of Olives on the route to Jericho. Translations vary slightly, including 'to Bahurim,' 'in Bahurim,' and 'of Bahurim,' but all denote the same locality. This consistent usage as a place name rather than a generic noun highlights its importance as a geographical and narrative setting within the biblical text.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding בַּחֻרִים as 'young men's village' rooted in the concept of chosen youth invites reflection on God's calling and selection of His people. The place name reminds believers that God often works through those who are chosen and set apart, symbolized by youthfulness and vigor. This aligns with the biblical theme of God raising up individuals and communities for His purposes. In the Christian faith, it underscores the call to be 'chosen' in Christ, living with vitality and purpose as God's people in the world.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Samuel 3:16, the narrative describes a man weeping as he follows a woman 'to Bahurim,' emphasizing the emotional weight of the moment. The mention of Bahurim situates the event in a real, tangible place, grounding the story in historical reality. The word בַּחֻרִים here not only identifies the location but also evokes the idea of a community of chosen youth, perhaps underscoring the human drama unfolding within God's providential plan.
